paper_a.title: Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting

paper_b.title: Regularization of Neural Networks using DropConnect

metadata.description: DropConnect (paper B) explicitly generalizes Dropout (paper A): both inject independent multiplicative Bernoulli noise as a regularizer, but Dropout masks unit activations whereas DropConnect masks individual weight entries — Dropout is the row-structured-mask special case (paper B's RP221.2 makes this explicit). Paper B inherits paper A's Bernoulli-mask SGD recipe and exponential-model-averaging philosophy, then adds (i) a Gaussian moment-matching inference rule that paper A introduces only as a noise-distribution alternative, and (ii) a Rademacher-complexity generalization bound absent from paper A.

matches.explanation: Both define the standard Dropout operation as element-wise multiplication of layer activations by an independent Bernoulli(p) mask. Paper B's DP221.4 is annotated origin=external citing Hinton et al. 2012, i.e. paper B explicitly imports paper A's contribution as prior work — direct evidence for the EXT relation.

DP220.4 is paper A's per-layer dropout feed-forward operation (mask the activations). DP221.5 is paper B's DropConnect layer (mask the weights). They play the exact same architectural role — a single regularized linear+activation stage with an injected Bernoulli(p) mask — but the mask lives on activations vs. on weight entries. This is the central A-vs-B contrast and the substantive content of the EXT generalization.

Both formalize the network-as-mixture viewpoint: paper A's 'Thinned Network' describes the trained net as a collection of $2^n$ unit-mask subnetworks sharing weights; paper B's 'DropConnect Network' writes the same idea as $o = E_M[f(x;\theta,M)]$ summed over $2^{|M|}$ weight masks. Same conceptual role (model-mixture interpretation), different combinatorial scope (unit masks vs. connection masks).

Both are the per-example SGD training procedure: sample a fresh Bernoulli mask, forward and backprop through the masked network, update parameters. Paper A's AP220.1 additionally bakes in max-norm projection and a thinned-net interpretation; paper B's AP221.1 is a leaner SGD wrapper around the masked-weight forward/backward. Same algorithmic skeleton, mask-target differs as in DP220.4 vs DP221.5.

Composite L2-vs-L2 step alignment under the AP220.1 ↔ AP221.1 parent match. Paper A decomposes training into 5 steps (sample masks, forward on thinned net, backprop on thinned net, max-norm projection, set test-time scaled net); paper B compresses the same logic into 2 steps (forward with mask + backprop with masked gradient $W \leftarrow W - \eta(M \star A'_W)$). The mask-sampling, forward, and masked-backprop steps correspond directly; paper A's max-norm and test-time-scaling steps have no paper-B counterpart at the algorithm-step level.

Both describe Monte-Carlo / mean-field model averaging at test time as the baseline approximation to the exponential mixture. AP220.2 averages predictions of $k$ dropout-sampled networks; AP221.3 (origin=external, citing Hinton et al. 2012) describes the Hinton-style averaging $\sum_M a((M\star W)v) \approx a(\sum_M (M\star W)v)$. Paper B treats this as the baseline that its Gaussian moment-matching inference improves upon.

Both papers' test-time inference rules trade off exact mixture computation against tractability. Paper A: test-time weight scaling $W_{test}=pW$ (DP220.5) is justified as approximating the equally-weighted geometric mean of $2^n$ thinned networks (ClP220.1); the expected-output / matched-mean argument is the same logic paper B formalizes as Gaussian moment matching. Paper B's AP221.2 with sub-steps ASP221.3-5 and the moments $E_M[u]=pWv$, $V_M[u]=p(1-p)(W\star W)(v\star v)$ (EP221.2) generalizes the mean-only weight-scaling trick to a Gaussian sample-and-activate scheme. Many-to-many cluster correspondence.

Paper A's Gaussian-dropout alternative (DP220.9) replaces Bernoulli with $\mathcal{N}(1,\sigma^2)$ multiplicative noise on activations, with the moment-matching identity $\sigma^2=(1-p)/p$ giving the same first two moments (ClP220.2). Paper B's EP221.2 uses the analogous moment-matched Gaussian over the weight-mask sum $u=\sum_j W_{ij}v_j M_{ij}$ at inference. Both papers reach for a Gaussian moment-match approximation but use it for different purposes (training noise vs. test-time inference) and on different quantities (activations vs. pre-activation weighted sums).

Paper A explicitly poses the regularization-and-cheap-model-averaging problem as its motivating problem statement; paper B does not lift this to a separate problem-type node, treating it as implicit motivation.

Paper A defines the standard (no-dropout) feed-forward operation as a baseline before introducing dropout. Paper B does not extract this baseline as a separate definition — it is folded implicitly into DP221.5 / DP221.6.

Paper A's RBM extension (Dropout RBM definition, RBM joint, dropout-RBM conditional, CD-1 learning algorithm with mask, RBM features experiment) is paper-A-specific. Paper B has no graphical-model thread; this is a paper A extension to the unsupervised-pretraining setting that DropConnect does not address.
Paper A's dropout-finetuning-of-pretrained-networks recipe (scale weights by $1/p$, fine-tune with small learning rate) has no DropConnect counterpart; paper B does not address pretraining.

Paper A's marginalized-dropout-as-ridge-regression analysis (linear-regression problem, the proposition equating expected dropout loss to ridge with feature-std penalty, both forms of the closed-form objective, and the proof) is a paper-A-specific theoretical contribution. Paper B's theoretical apparatus is Rademacher generalization bounds — a different mathematical lens.

Paper B's headline theoretical contribution — empirical Rademacher complexity of the DropConnect network is linear in keep probability $p$ (theorem, generalization bound equation, proof, layer-bound remark) — has no counterpart in paper A. Paper A reports no generalization bounds. (Note: paper-B-side none entries listed under paper_a_nodes=[].)

Paper B's Rademacher-bound supporting lemmas (logistic-loss properties, activation-composition bound, network-layer bound, expectation-class Rademacher bound, and proofs of the latter two) have no paper-A counterpart for the same reason: paper A pursues no Rademacher-style theory.

Paper B's full four-component model (CNN feature extractor + DropConnect layer + softmax + cross-entropy) is the wrapper architecture in which the bound is proved; paper A discusses dropout as a layer-agnostic recipe rather than committing to a specific feature-extractor + classifier composition.
Paper B introduces a logistic-loss definition needed for its generalization-bound machinery; paper A does not lift its loss to a separate node.

RP221.2 is the paper B remark stating 'DropConnect generalizes Dropout' — when $a(0)=0$, dropout's $r=m\star a(Wv)$ equals $a(m\star W v)$, a row-structured weight mask. This remark is paper-B's own articulation of the EXT relationship; paper A naturally has no such cross-reference. It is the strongest single piece of textual evidence for relation_type=EXT.

Both papers' MNIST classification benchmark, used as the canonical demonstration of the regularizer. Paper A: 1.35% (dropout, plain) down to 0.79% (DBM-pretrained); paper B: 1.20% (relu) and 0.21% (deeper Ciresan-style extractor).

CIFAR-10 and SVHN ConvNet image-classification benchmarks reported in both papers as standard regularizer evaluations. Paper A reports CIFAR-10 (14.32%/12.61%) and SVHN (3.02%/2.55%); paper B reports CIFAR-10 (9.41% with voting) and SVHN (1.94% with voting). Same datasets, comparable role in each paper's empirical section.
